items.name: Highest Test innings
items.blurb: Brian Lara of the West Indies made 400 not out against England in Antigua in 2004, ten years after his previous record of 375. Matthew Hayden's 380 had held the record for six months in between.

items.name: Highest first-class innings
items.blurb: Brian Lara made 501 not out for Warwickshire against Durham at Edgbaston in 1994, beating Hanif Mohammad's 499.

items.name: Most Test runs
items.blurb: Sachin Tendulkar of India scored 15,921 runs in 200 Tests (1989–2013). Joe Root was the closest active player as of 2025.

items.name: Most Test wickets
items.blurb: Muttiah Muralitharan of Sri Lanka took exactly 800 Test wickets, the last with his final ball in Test cricket in 2010. Shane Warne (708) is second.

items.name: Highest Test batting average
items.blurb: Don Bradman of Australia averaged 99.94 in 52 Tests. He needed only four runs in his last innings in 1948 to average 100, but was out for a duck.

items.name: Test centuries record
items.blurb: Sachin Tendulkar scored 51 Test centuries, the record as of 2025; Jacques Kallis is next with 45.

items.name: Highest Test team total
items.blurb: Sri Lanka made 952 for 6 declared against India in Colombo in 1997. Sanath Jayasuriya scored 340 of them.

items.name: Lowest Test team total
items.blurb: New Zealand were all out for 26 against England in Auckland in 1955. It is still the lowest Test total.

items.name: Fastest Test century
items.blurb: New Zealand captain Brendon McCullum reached 100 off 54 balls against Australia in Christchurch in his final Test in 2016, beating the 56-ball record of Viv Richards and Misbah-ul-Haq.

items.name: Best Test innings bowling
items.blurb: England off-spinner Jim Laker took 10 for 53 against Australia at Old Trafford in 1956, and 19 wickets in the match. Anil Kumble and Ajaz Patel have also taken all ten in an innings.

items.name: Highest ODI innings
items.blurb: Rohit Sharma of India scored 264 against Sri Lanka in Kolkata in 2014. It was still the highest ODI score as of 2025.

items.name: ODI runs record
items.blurb: Sachin Tendulkar scored 18,426 runs in 463 one-day internationals (1989–2012), the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most men's international goals
items.blurb: Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo passed Ali Daei's 109 goals in 2021 and was still adding to his record as of 2025.

items.name: Most women's international goals
items.blurb: Canada's Christine Sinclair scored 190 international goals before retiring from international football in 2023, more than any player, man or woman.

items.name: Most women's World Cup goals
items.blurb: Brazil's Marta scored 17 goals at Women's World Cups, the record as of 2025; Birgit Prinz of Germany has 14.

items.name: Most men's World Cup titles
items.blurb: Brazil won the men's World Cup five times (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002), the record as of 2025. Germany and Italy have four each.

items.name: Most men's World Cup matches played
items.record: Most men's World Cup matches played
items.blurb: Lionel Messi played his 26th World Cup match in the 2022 final, passing Lothar Matthäus's 25. It was the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most Ballon d'Or wins
items.blurb: Lionel Messi won the Ballon d'Or eight times (2009–2023). Cristiano Ronaldo won five. Messi's eight were the record as of 2025.

items.name: Biggest win in men's international football
items.record: Biggest win in men's international football
items.blurb: Australia beat American Samoa 31–0 in a World Cup qualifier in Coffs Harbour in 2001. Archie Thompson scored 13 goals, also a record for an international match.

items.name: Fastest World Cup goal
items.blurb: Turkey's Hakan Şükür scored after about 11 seconds against South Korea in the third-place match at the 2002 World Cup.

items.name: Most Premier League goals
items.blurb: Alan Shearer scored 260 Premier League goals for Blackburn Rovers and Newcastle United (1992–2006). It was still the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most European Cup / Champions League titles
items.record: Most European Cup / Champions League titles
items.blurb: Real Madrid won their 15th European Cup in 2024, the record as of 2025. AC Milan are next with seven.

items.name: Most men's Rugby World Cup titles
items.record: Most men's Rugby World Cup titles
items.blurb: South Africa won the Rugby World Cup in 1995, 2007, 2019 and 2023, four titles, the record as of 2025. New Zealand have three.

items.name: Most points in men's Test rugby
items.record: Most points in men's Test rugby
items.blurb: New Zealand fly-half Dan Carter scored 1,598 Test points (2003–2015), the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most points at men's Rugby World Cups
items.record: Most points at men's Rugby World Cups
items.blurb: England's Jonny Wilkinson scored 277 points at four Rugby World Cups (1999–2011), the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most men's Grand Slam singles titles
items.record: Most men's Grand Slam singles titles
items.blurb: Novak Djokovic of Serbia won 24 Grand Slam singles titles, the men's record as of 2025. Rafael Nadal won 22 and Roger Federer 20.

items.name: Most Grand Slam singles titles (all-time)
items.blurb: Australia's Margaret Court won 24 Grand Slam singles titles (1960–1973), many before the Open Era began in 1968. Serena Williams holds the Open Era record with 23.

items.name: Most Grand Slam singles titles in the Open Era (women)
items.record: Most Grand Slam singles titles in the Open Era (women)
items.blurb: Serena Williams won 23 Grand Slam singles titles from 1999 to 2017, the Open Era record. Steffi Graf won 22.

items.name: Most French Open singles titles
items.blurb: Rafael Nadal of Spain won the French Open 14 times between 2005 and 2022, the most titles anyone has won at one Grand Slam.

items.name: Most men's Wimbledon singles titles
items.blurb: Roger Federer won eight Wimbledon singles titles (2003–2017), the men's record as of 2025. Novak Djokovic has seven.

items.name: Most women's Wimbledon singles titles
items.blurb: Martina Navratilova won nine Wimbledon singles titles, the last in 1990.

items.name: Longest tennis match
items.blurb: John Isner beat Nicolas Mahut 70–68 in the fifth set at Wimbledon in 2010, over three days and 11 hours 5 minutes of play. Tie-breaks in final sets were brought in later, partly because of it.

items.name: Most men's major golf titles
items.blurb: Jack Nicklaus won 18 majors between 1962 and 1986, the last at the 1986 Masters aged 46. Tiger Woods is second with 15.

items.name: Masters titles record
items.blurb: Jack Nicklaus won the Masters six times (1963–1986). Tiger Woods has five.

items.name: Biggest winning margin in a men's major
items.record: Biggest winning margin in a men's major
items.blurb: Tiger Woods won the 2000 US Open at Pebble Beach by 15 strokes, the largest winning margin in a men's major championship.

items.name: Lowest round on the PGA Tour
items.record: Lowest round on the PGA Tour
items.blurb: Jim Furyk shot 58 (12 under par) at the Travelers Championship in 2016, the lowest PGA Tour round as of 2025. He had also shot 59 in 2013.

items.name: Most Formula One race wins
items.blurb: Lewis Hamilton passed Michael Schumacher's 91 wins in 2020 and had 105 wins as of 2025 (the end of that season), the record.

items.name: F1 pole positions record
items.blurb: Lewis Hamilton had 104 Formula One pole positions, the record as of 2025. Michael Schumacher had 68 and Ayrton Senna 65.

items.name: Most Formula One wins in a season
items.record: Most Formula One wins in a season
items.blurb: Max Verstappen won 19 of the 22 Grands Prix in 2023, the record as of 2025.

items.name: Youngest Formula One world champion
items.blurb: Sebastian Vettel won the 2010 title aged 23 years and 134 days, still the youngest champion as of 2025.

items.name: Most Formula One constructors' titles
items.blurb: Ferrari won 16 constructors' championships, the last in 2008. It was still the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most NBA career points
items.blurb: LeBron James passed Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's 38,387 points in February 2023 and was still adding to the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most points in an NBA game
items.record: Most points in an NBA game
items.blurb: Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 points for the Philadelphia Warriors against the New York Knicks on 2 March 1962. Kobe Bryant's 81 in 2006 is the next best.

items.name: Most NBA championships
items.blurb: The Boston Celtics won their 18th NBA title in 2024, one more than the Los Angeles Lakers. It was the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most NBA titles by a player
items.record: Most NBA titles by a player
items.blurb: Bill Russell won 11 NBA titles with the Boston Celtics in 13 seasons (1957–1969), the last two as player-coach.

items.name: Most NHL career points
items.blurb: Wayne Gretzky scored 2,857 points (894 goals and 1,963 assists) in the NHL. His assists alone would have been enough for the points record.

items.name: Most NHL career goals
items.blurb: Alex Ovechkin passed Wayne Gretzky's 894 NHL goals in April 2025 and held the record as of 2025.

items.name: NHL single-season goals record
items.record: Most goals in an NHL season
items.blurb: Wayne Gretzky scored 92 goals in the 1981–82 season, the NHL record.

items.name: Most Stanley Cups
items.blurb: The Montreal Canadiens won 24 Stanley Cups, the last in 1993. It was still the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most MLB career home runs
items.blurb: Barry Bonds hit 762 home runs (1986–2007), passing Hank Aaron's 755 in 2007. It was still the record as of 2025.

items.name: MLB single-season home run record
items.record: Most home runs in an MLB season
items.blurb: Barry Bonds hit 73 home runs in 2001, the single-season record as of 2025.

items.name: Most MLB career hits
items.blurb: Pete Rose collected 4,256 hits (1963–1986), passing Ty Cobb in 1985.

items.name: Most MLB pitching wins
items.blurb: Cy Young won 511 games between 1890 and 1911. The award for the best pitcher each season is named after him.

items.name: Most World Series titles
items.blurb: The New York Yankees won 27 World Series, the last in 2009. It was the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most consecutive MLB games played
items.blurb: Cal Ripken Jr. of the Baltimore Orioles played 2,632 games in a row (1982–1998), breaking Lou Gehrig's 2,130.

items.name: Most Super Bowl wins by a player
items.record: Most Super Bowl wins by a player
items.blurb: Quarterback Tom Brady won seven Super Bowls, six with New England and one with Tampa Bay, the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most NFL career receiving yards
items.blurb: Jerry Rice gained 22,895 receiving yards (1985–2004), over 5,000 more than anyone else.

items.name: Most NFL career rushing yards
items.blurb: Emmitt Smith ran for 18,355 yards (1990–2004), mostly with the Dallas Cowboys, passing Walter Payton in 2002.

items.name: Most VFL/AFL career goals
items.blurb: Tony Lockett kicked 1,360 goals for St Kilda and Sydney (1983–2002), passing Gordon Coventry's 1,299 in 1999.

items.name: Most VFL/AFL games
items.blurb: North Melbourne's Brent Harvey played 432 games (1996–2016), passing Michael Tuck's 426.

items.name: Most goals in a VFL/AFL game
items.record: Most goals in a VFL/AFL game
items.blurb: Melbourne's Fred Fanning kicked 18 goals (and 1 behind) against St Kilda in 1947. Nobody has matched it in VFL/AFL football.

items.name: Most Olympic medals
items.blurb: American swimmer Michael Phelps won 28 Olympic medals, 23 of them gold, at five Games from 2004 to 2016.

items.name: Olympic gold medals record
items.blurb: Michael Phelps won 23 Olympic gold medals. No one else has won more than nine.

items.name: Most golds at one Games
items.record: Most gold medals at one Olympics
items.blurb: Michael Phelps won eight golds at Beijing 2008, beating Mark Spitz's seven at Munich 1972.

items.name: Most Olympic medals by a woman (Summer)
items.record: Most Olympic medals by a woman (Summer)
items.blurb: Soviet gymnast Larisa Latynina won 18 Olympic medals (1956–1964). She held the overall record until Michael Phelps passed it in 2012.

items.name: Oldest Olympic medallist
items.blurb: Oscar Swahn won silver in a team shooting event at Antwerp 1920 aged 72, the oldest Olympic medallist.

items.name: Most World Cup alpine wins (men)
items.blurb: Sweden's Ingemar Stenmark won 86 World Cup races (1974–1989), the men's record as of 2025.

items.name: Most World Cup alpine wins (all)
items.blurb: Mikaela Shiffrin passed Ingemar Stenmark's 86 wins in 2023 and reached 100 in 2025, the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most consecutive world heavyweight title defences
items.record: Most consecutive world heavyweight title defences
items.blurb: Joe Louis held the world heavyweight title from 1937 to 1949 and defended it 25 times.

items.name: Most Tour de France stage wins
items.record: Most Tour de France stage wins
items.blurb: Britain's Mark Cavendish won his 35th Tour de France stage in 2024, passing Eddy Merckx's 34.

items.name: Most PDC/BDO world darts titles
items.blurb: Phil "The Power" Taylor won 16 world darts championships (two BDO, 14 PDC) between 1990 and 2013.

items.name: Fastest snooker maximum (147)
items.blurb: Ronnie O'Sullivan made a 147 in 5 minutes 8 seconds at the 1997 World Championship, the fastest maximum in competition.

items.name: Highest classical chess rating
items.blurb: Magnus Carlsen of Norway reached a FIDE rating of 2882 in 2014, the highest classical rating ever. Garry Kasparov's peak was 2851.

items.name: Most sumo top-division titles
items.blurb: Mongolian-born Hakuhō won 45 top-division championships (2006–2021). The previous record was Taihō's 32.

items.name: Men's cycling hour record
items.blurb: Filippo Ganna of Italy rode 56.792 km in one hour in Grenchen, Switzerland in 2022. It was still the record as of 2025.

items.name: Mount Everest
items.blurb: Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and China, is 8,849 m above sea level by the 2020 China–Nepal survey. Older surveys gave 8,848 m.

items.name: K2
items.blurb: K2, on the border of Pakistan and China, is 8,611 m high. Climbers call it the Savage Mountain because so many have died on it.

items.name: Kangchenjunga
items.blurb: Kangchenjunga, on the border of Nepal and India, is 8,586 m high. It was thought to be the highest mountain until 1852.

items.name: Mount Kilimanjaro
items.blurb: Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania rises to 5,895 m. It is the highest free-standing mountain in the world.

items.name: Aconcagua
items.blurb: Aconcagua in Argentina is 6,961 m high, the highest mountain outside Asia and in both the Western and Southern Hemispheres.

items.name: Denali
items.blurb: Denali in Alaska is 6,190 m high by a 2015 survey. Its base-to-peak rise of about 5,500 m is one of the largest on land.

items.name: Mont Blanc
items.blurb: Mont Blanc, on the border of France and Italy, is about 4,806 m high. Its icy summit changes height by a metre or two from year to year.

items.name: Mount Vinson
items.blurb: Mount Vinson in the Ellsworth Mountains is 4,892 m high, the highest point in Antarctica.

items.name: Mount Kosciuszko
items.record: Highest mountain on the Australian mainland
items.blurb: Mount Kosciuszko in New South Wales is 2,228 m high. Australia's highest peak overall is Mawson Peak (2,745 m) on Heard Island, an external territory.

items.name: Aoraki / Mount Cook
items.blurb: Aoraki / Mount Cook is 3,724 m high. A rock and ice fall in 1991 took about 10 m off its summit, and erosion later took more.

items.name: Mount Fuji
items.blurb: Mount Fuji, an active volcano on Honshu, is 3,776 m high. It last erupted in 1707.

items.name: Puncak Jaya
items.blurb: Puncak Jaya in Indonesian New Guinea is about 4,884 m high, the highest island peak in the world.

items.name: Mauna Kea
items.record: Tallest mountain from base to peak
items.blurb: Mauna Kea in Hawaii is only 4,207 m above sea level, but measured from its base on the Pacific floor it rises over 10,000 m, more than Everest.

items.name: Chimborazo
items.blurb: Chimborazo in Ecuador is only 6,263 m above sea level, but it sits on the equatorial bulge, so its summit is about 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's.

items.name: Gangkhar Puensum
items.blurb: Gangkhar Puensum in Bhutan, about 7,570 m high, has never been climbed. Bhutan has banned climbing mountains over 6,000 m since 2003.

items.name: Andes
items.blurb: The Andes run about 7,000 km down the western side of South America, through seven countries.

items.name: Nile
items.blurb: The Nile is about 6,650 km long. It is usually listed as the longest river in the world, although some measurements make the Amazon longer.

items.name: Amazon
items.blurb: The Amazon pours about 200,000 cubic metres of water a second into the Atlantic, more than the next seven largest rivers together.

items.name: Yangtze
items.blurb: The Yangtze in China is about 6,300 km long, the longest river in Asia and the longest flowing entirely within one country.

items.name: Volga
items.blurb: The Volga flows about 3,530 km through Russia to the Caspian Sea, the longest river in Europe.

items.name: Murray River
items.blurb: The Murray River is about 2,508 km long, from the Australian Alps to the sea in South Australia.

items.name: River Severn
items.record: Longest river in the United Kingdom
items.blurb: The River Severn is about 354 km long, rising in Wales and flowing through England. The Thames is close behind at about 346 km.

items.name: Congo River
items.blurb: The Congo River is over 220 m deep in places, the deepest river measured. It is also the second-longest river in Africa, about 4,700 km.

items.name: Caspian Sea
items.blurb: The Caspian Sea covers about 371,000 km². It is called a sea because it is salty, but it has no outlet to the ocean, which makes it a lake.

items.name: Lake Superior
items.blurb: Lake Superior, on the border of the USA and Canada, covers about 82,100 km². Lake Baikal holds more water, but Superior is bigger on the map.

items.name: Lake Baikal
items.blurb: Lake Baikal in Siberia is 1,642 m deep. It holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth's surface and is also the oldest lake, about 25 million years old.

items.name: Lake Tanganyika
items.blurb: Lake Tanganyika is about 1,470 m deep and 673 km long, the longest freshwater lake in the world. Four countries share it.

items.name: Lake Victoria
items.blurb: Lake Victoria, shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania, is the largest lake in Africa and the largest tropical lake in the world.

items.name: Lake Ladoga
items.blurb: Lake Ladoga covers about 17,700 km², the largest lake entirely in Europe.

items.name: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre
items.blurb: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre is Australia's largest lake and lowest point, about 15 m below sea level. It fills completely only a few times a century.

items.name: Dead Sea
items.blurb: The shore of the Dead Sea, between Israel, the West Bank and Jordan, is about 430 m below sea level, and it drops about a metre a year as the water level falls.

items.name: Pacific Ocean
items.blurb: The Pacific Ocean covers about a third of Earth's surface, more than all the land put together.

items.name: Arctic Ocean
items.blurb: The Arctic Ocean, around the North Pole, is the smallest and shallowest ocean. Much of it is covered by sea ice.

items.name: Challenger Deep
items.blurb: The Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench of the western Pacific, is about 10,935 m deep. Surveys differ by tens of metres.

items.name: Milwaukee Deep
items.blurb: The Milwaukee Deep in the Puerto Rico Trench is about 8,400 m deep, the deepest point in the Atlantic.

items.name: Molloy Deep
items.record: Deepest point in the Arctic Ocean
items.blurb: The Molloy Deep in the Fram Strait is about 5,550 m deep, the deepest point in the Arctic Ocean.

items.name: Great Barrier Reef
items.blurb: The Great Barrier Reef off Queensland, Australia, stretches about 2,300 km and is made of nearly 3,000 separate reefs. It can be seen from space.

items.name: Bay of Bengal
items.blurb: The Bay of Bengal in the northeast Indian Ocean covers about 2.2 million km², the largest bay in the world.

items.name: Antarctic Desert
items.blurb: Antarctica gets so little snow each year that scientists count it as a desert, about 14 million km², bigger than the Sahara.

items.name: Sahara
items.blurb: The Sahara covers about 9.2 million km² of North Africa, nearly as big as the United States.

items.name: Atacama Desert
items.blurb: Parts of the Atacama Desert in Chile have had almost no rain for centuries. NASA has tested Mars rovers there.

items.name: Great Victoria Desert
items.blurb: The Great Victoria Desert, in Western Australia and South Australia, covers about 349,000 km².

items.name: Rub' al Khali
items.blurb: The Rub' al Khali, or Empty Quarter, covers about 650,000 km² of Saudi Arabia, Oman, the UAE and Yemen, almost all of it sand.

items.name: Greenland
items.blurb: Greenland covers about 2.1 million km² (sources differ slightly), most of it under an ice sheet. Australia is bigger but counts as a continent.

items.name: New Guinea
items.blurb: New Guinea covers about 780,000 km² and is shared by Papua New Guinea and Indonesia. It has over 800 languages.

items.name: Borneo
items.blurb: Borneo covers about 730,000 km², the largest island in Asia. It is the only island shared by three countries.

items.name: Great Britain
items.blurb: Great Britain covers about 210,000–220,000 km², depending on how the coast is measured, the largest island in Europe and the ninth-largest in the world.

items.name: Sicily
items.blurb: Sicily, at the toe of Italy, covers about 25,700 km². Mount Etna is on it.

items.name: Cuba
items.blurb: The main island of Cuba covers about 105,000 km², the largest in the Caribbean.

items.name: K'gari
items.blurb: K'gari, formerly Fraser Island, is about 120 km long and made almost entirely of sand, with rainforest growing on it.

items.name: Manitoulin Island
items.blurb: Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron, Canada, covers about 2,766 km². It even has lakes of its own, with islands in them.

items.name: Angel Falls
items.blurb: Angel Falls in Venezuela drops 979 m in total, with an unbroken plunge of 807 m.

items.name: Victoria Falls
items.blurb: Victoria Falls, on the Zambezi between Zambia and Zimbabwe, is 1,708 m wide and 108 m high, the largest single curtain of falling water.

items.name: Khone Phapheng Falls
items.blurb: Khone Phapheng Falls on the Mekong River in Laos are about 10.8 km wide, a maze of channels and cascades.

items.name: Veryovkina Cave
items.blurb: Veryovkina Cave in the Arabika Massif of the western Caucasus was explored to about 2,212 m deep in 2018.

items.name: Mammoth Cave
items.blurb: Mammoth Cave in Kentucky has more than 680 km of mapped passages, and explorers keep finding more.

items.name: Hang Sơn Đoòng
items.blurb: Hang Sơn Đoòng in Vietnam, explored in 2009, has a passage over 5 km long and up to 200 m high, with its own jungle and clouds.

items.name: Mauna Loa
items.blurb: Mauna Loa in Hawaii makes up about half of the Big Island. It last erupted in 2022.

items.name: Ojos del Salado
items.blurb: Ojos del Salado rises to 6,893 m on the border of Chile and Argentina. It is the highest volcano on Earth.

items.name: Mount Tambora
items.blurb: Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted in 1815. Its ash cooled the world so much that 1816 became the "Year Without a Summer".

items.name: Strongest earthquake recorded
items.blurb: The earthquake near Valdivia, Chile, on 22 May 1960 measured about magnitude 9.5, the most powerful ever recorded.

items.name: Lituya Bay
items.blurb: In 1958 an earthquake shook a rockslide into Lituya Bay, Alaska. The wave stripped trees from the slope opposite up to 524 m above the water.

items.name: Vredefort crater
items.blurb: The Vredefort crater in South Africa was about 170–300 km across when it formed about two billion years ago. Erosion has worn most of it away.

items.name: Hoba meteorite
items.blurb: The Hoba meteorite in Namibia weighs about 60 tonnes and is mostly iron. It is too heavy to move, so it stays where it was found in 1920.

items.name: Lowest air temperature recorded
items.blurb: The Soviet Vostok Station in Antarctica recorded −89.2 °C on 21 July 1983, the official world record low (WMO).

items.name: Highest air temperature officially recognised
items.blurb: Furnace Creek in Death Valley, California, recorded 56.7 °C on 10 July 1913. The WMO still lists it as the world record, though some climate scientists doubt the reading.

items.name: Highest temperature recorded in the UK
items.record: Highest temperature recorded in the UK
items.blurb: Coningsby in Lincolnshire reached 40.3 °C on 19 July 2022, the first time the UK passed 40 °C.

items.name: Coldest temperature recorded in the Northern Hemisphere
items.record: Coldest temperature recorded in the Northern Hemisphere
items.blurb: An automatic weather station at Klinck on the Greenland ice sheet recorded −69.6 °C on 22 December 1991, confirmed by the WMO in 2020.

items.name: Strongest wind gust recorded (not a tornado)
items.record: Strongest wind gust recorded (not a tornado)
items.blurb: Barrow Island off Western Australia recorded a 408 km/h gust during Cyclone Olivia on 10 April 1996, the WMO record for a non-tornado gust.

items.name: Most rain in 24 hours
items.blurb: During Tropical Cyclone Denise in January 1966, 1,825 mm of rain fell in 24 hours on the French island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean. Sources name the spot as Cilaos or Foc-Foc.

items.name: Largest hailstone recorded
items.blurb: A hailstone 20 cm across and weighing 0.88 kg fell at Vivian, South Dakota on 23 July 2010, the record for both size and weight.

items.name: Lowest sea-level pressure recorded
items.blurb: Typhoon Tip over the western Pacific reached a central pressure of 870 hPa on 12 October 1979. It was also the largest tropical cyclone recorded, about 2,220 km across.

items.name: Longest-lasting tropical cyclone
items.blurb: Cyclone Freddy formed off northern Australia in February 2023 and crossed the whole Indian Ocean to hit Madagascar and Mozambique twice, lasting about 36 days.

items.name: Hyperion
items.blurb: Hyperion, a coast redwood in Redwood National Park, is about 116 m tall. Its exact location is kept secret to protect it.

items.name: Tallest tree species
items.blurb: Coast redwoods grow along the foggy coast of northern California and can reach over 115 m, taller than any other tree.

items.name: General Sherman
items.blurb: General Sherman, a giant sequoia in California, holds about 1,500 cubic metres of wood. It is not the tallest tree, but it is the biggest.

items.name: Oldest known non-clonal tree species
items.blurb: Great Basin bristlecone pines grow in the high mountains of the western USA. One called Methuselah is over 4,800 years old.

items.name: Largest single flower
items.blurb: Rafflesia arnoldii of Sumatra and Borneo has flowers up to about a metre across. It is a parasite with no leaves and smells of rotting meat.

items.name: Largest unbranched inflorescence
items.blurb: The titan arum of Sumatra grows a flower spike up to 3 m tall that smells of rotting flesh to attract insects.

items.name: Largest seed
items.blurb: The coco de mer palm of the Seychelles has seeds weighing up to about 18 kg, the largest and heaviest of any plant.

items.name: Largest tree-borne fruit
items.blurb: Jackfruit, native to South and Southeast Asia, can weigh up to about 50 kg. Watermelons and pumpkins are bigger but grow on vines.

items.name: Smallest flowering plant
items.blurb: Wolffia, a kind of duckweed, is less than 2 mm long. Its flower is so small it can hardly be seen.

items.name: Largest rainforest
items.blurb: The Amazon rainforest covers about 5.5 million km² across nine countries, about 60% of it in Brazil.

items.name: Largest land biome
items.blurb: The taiga, or boreal forest, rings the far north of the world and is the largest land biome.

items.name: Lightest element
items.blurb: Hydrogen, element 1, is the lightest element. It is also the most common element in the universe.

items.name: Commonest element in the universe
items.record: Most abundant element in the universe
items.blurb: About three-quarters of the normal matter in the universe, by mass, is hydrogen. Helium makes up most of the rest.

items.name: Most abundant element in Earth's crust
items.record: Most abundant element in Earth's crust
items.blurb: Oxygen makes up about 46% of Earth's crust by mass, locked in rocks and minerals. Silicon is second.

items.name: Lowest boiling point of any element
items.record: Lowest boiling point of any element
items.blurb: Helium boils at about −268.9 °C, only about 4 degrees above absolute zero. It never freezes at normal pressure.

items.name: Most electronegative element
items.blurb: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (3.98 on the Pauling scale), which makes it the most reactive non-metal.

items.name: Highest atomic number (named element)
items.blurb: Oganesson, element 118, was first made in 2002 and named in 2016 after the physicist Yuri Oganessian. Only a handful of its atoms have ever existed.

items.name: Rarest naturally occurring element
items.blurb: Astatine forms only briefly as uranium and thorium decay. At any moment there is less than a gram of it in Earth's crust.

items.name: Most abundant gas in the atmosphere
items.record: Most abundant gas in the atmosphere
items.blurb: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere; oxygen is about 21%.

items.name: Highest melting point of any metal
items.record: Highest melting point of any metal
items.blurb: Tungsten melts at about 3,422 °C, the highest of any metal. That is why it was used for light bulb filaments.

items.name: Lowest melting point of any metal
items.record: Lowest melting point of any metal
items.blurb: Mercury melts at −38.83 °C, so it is liquid at room temperature. Gallium melts at about 30 °C, in your hand.

items.name: Lightest metal
items.blurb: Lithium has about half the density of water. It is used in rechargeable batteries.

items.name: Best electrical conductor
items.blurb: Silver conducts electricity slightly better than copper, but copper is used for wires because it is much cheaper.

items.name: Most abundant metal in Earth's crust
items.record: Most abundant metal in Earth's crust
items.blurb: Aluminium makes up about 8% of Earth's crust by mass, the most of any metal. Iron is second.

items.name: Most produced metal
items.blurb: Iron makes up about 90% of all the metal refined in the world, nearly all of it turned into steel.

items.name: Hardest mineral on the Mohs scale
items.record: Hardest mineral on the Mohs scale
items.blurb: Diamond, a form of pure carbon, is rated 10, the top of the Mohs scale. Almost nothing but another diamond can scratch it.

items.name: Softest mineral on the Mohs scale
items.record: Softest mineral on the Mohs scale
items.blurb: Talc, used in talcum powder, is rated 1 on the Mohs scale. You can scratch it with a fingernail.

items.name: Mohs 9 mineral
items.blurb: Corundum, crystalline aluminium oxide, is rated 9 on the Mohs scale. Red corundum is ruby; other colours are sapphire.

items.name: Largest gem-quality rough diamond
items.blurb: The Cullinan Diamond, found in South Africa in 1905, weighed 3,106 carats (621 g). Its two biggest pieces are in the British Crown Jewels.

items.name: Largest cut and faceted diamond
items.blurb: The Golden Jubilee Diamond weighs 545.67 carats. It was cut in the 1990s and given to King Bhumibol of Thailand for his golden jubilee.

items.name: Largest alluvial gold nugget
items.blurb: The Welcome Stranger was found just below the surface at Moliagul, Victoria, in 1869. After trimming it yielded about 72 kg of pure gold.

items.name: Oldest known piece of Earth
items.blurb: Zircon grains from the Jack Hills in Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old, the oldest known material formed on Earth.

items.name: Most common mineral group in the crust
items.record: Most common mineral group in the crust
items.blurb: Feldspars make up roughly 40–60% of Earth's crust, depending on how it is counted. Quartz is the next most common mineral in the continental crust.

items.name: Most used building material
items.blurb: Concrete is the most used man-made material. Only water is used in greater amounts by people.

items.name: Most produced plastic
items.blurb: Polyethylene makes up about a third of all plastic produced. Shopping bags, milk bottles and cling film are made from it.

items.name: Lowest possible temperature
items.blurb: Absolute zero, 0 kelvin, is −273.15 °C. Nothing can be cooled to it exactly, only very close.

items.name: Coldest known natural place
items.blurb: Gas rushing out of the Boomerang Nebula has cooled to about 1 K (−272 °C), colder than the 2.7 K glow left over from the Big Bang.

items.name: Venus
items.blurb: Venus averages about 464 °C at the surface, hot enough to melt lead. Its thick carbon dioxide air traps heat, so it is hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun.

items.name: Uranus
items.blurb: Uranus has the coldest planetary atmosphere measured, about −224 °C, even though Neptune is farther from the Sun.

items.name: Hottest main type of star
items.blurb: O-type stars are blue and over 30,000 K at the surface. The Sun is a yellow G-type star, about 5,800 K, and red M-type stars are the coolest.

items.name: Hottest part of the Solar System
items.record: Hottest part of the Solar System
items.blurb: The Sun's core is about 15 million °C, where hydrogen fuses into helium. Its visible surface is only about 5,500 °C.

items.name: Hottest flame from a chemical
items.blurb: Dicyanoacetylene burns in oxygen at about 4,990 °C, the hottest flame known. An oxy-acetylene welding torch reaches about 3,500 °C.

items.name: Temperature of basalt lava
items.blurb: Basalt lava erupts at about 1,100–1,200 °C. Thicker lavas such as rhyolite are cooler, about 700–900 °C.

items.name: Hottest temperature made by people
items.blurb: Smashing lead ions together at the Large Hadron Collider near Geneva in 2012 made a quark–gluon plasma of about 5.5 trillion degrees.

items.name: Hottest chili pepper
items.blurb: Pepper X, bred by Ed Currie in South Carolina, averaged about 2.69 million Scoville heat units in 2023 tests, taking the record from his own Carolina Reaper. It was the record as of 2025, though independent test results have not been published.

items.name: Loudest sound in recorded history
items.blurb: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa in Indonesia was heard about 4,800 km away, on Rodrigues Island near Mauritius.

items.name: Loudest animal
items.blurb: Sperm whales make clicks of up to about 230 dB underwater, which they use to find squid in the dark.

items.name: Loudest musical instrument
items.blurb: The Boardwalk Hall Auditorium Organ in Atlantic City has over 33,000 pipes, and Guinness World Records lists it as the loudest instrument ever built.

items.name: Largest man-made explosion
items.blurb: The Soviet Tsar Bomba hydrogen bomb, tested over Novaya Zemlya on 30 October 1961, released about 50 megatons, over 3,000 times the Hiroshima bomb.

items.name: Sirius
items.record: Brightest star in the night sky
items.blurb: Sirius, the Dog Star, is the brightest star in the night sky. It is about 8.6 light years away.

items.name: Brightest planet in the night sky
items.record: Brightest planet in the night sky
items.blurb: Venus is the brightest planet and, after the Moon, the brightest natural object in the night sky. It is often called the morning or evening star.

items.name: Brightest supernova recorded
items.blurb: SN 1006 appeared in the constellation Lupus in 1006. Records from China, Egypt and Europe say it was bright enough to read by at night.

items.name: Burj Khalifa
items.blurb: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai, finished in 2010, is 828 m tall with 163 floors. It was still the tallest building as of 2025; the Jeddah Tower in Saudi Arabia is being built to beat it.

items.name: Merdeka 118
items.blurb: Merdeka 118 (also called the Merdeka Maybank Tower) in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, finished in 2023, is about 679 m tall, the second-tallest building as of 2025.

items.name: Shanghai Tower
items.blurb: The twisting Shanghai Tower, finished in 2015, is 632 m tall, the tallest building in China as of 2025.

items.name: One World Trade Center
items.record: Tallest building in the United States
items.blurb: One World Trade Center in New York is 541 m (1,776 ft) tall, a height chosen for the year of American independence. It was the tallest in the USA as of 2025.

items.name: Lakhta Center
items.blurb: The Lakhta Center in Saint Petersburg, Russia, finished in 2019, is about 462 m tall, the tallest building in Europe as of 2025.

items.name: Empire State Building
items.blurb: The Empire State Building opened in 1931 at 381 m to its roof and stayed the world's tallest building until the World Trade Center's north tower passed it in 1970.

items.name: Boeing Everett Factory
items.blurb: Boeing's factory in Everett, Washington, encloses about 13.4 million cubic metres. Jumbo jets are built inside it.

items.name: Tokyo Skytree
items.blurb: Tokyo Skytree, a broadcasting and observation tower finished in 2012, is 634 m tall, the tallest tower as of 2025.

items.name: Warsaw Radio Mast
items.blurb: The Warsaw Radio Mast was about 646 m tall when finished in 1974. It fell during maintenance in 1991; nothing taller was built until the Burj Khalifa.

items.name: Statue of Unity
items.blurb: The Statue of Unity in Gujarat, India, shows the independence leader Vallabhbhai Patel and is 182 m tall, about twice the Statue of Liberty with its base. It was the tallest statue as of 2025.

items.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
items.blurb: The Great Pyramid of Giza was about 146.6 m tall when finished around 2560 BC. Lincoln Cathedral's spire passed it in about 1311.

items.name: Great Pyramid of Cholula
items.blurb: The Great Pyramid of Cholula in Mexico has a base about four times the size of the Great Pyramid of Giza. A Spanish church was built on top of it.

items.name: Angkor Wat
items.blurb: Angkor Wat, built in the 1100s, covers about 162 hectares. It appears on Cambodia's flag.

items.name: Ain Dubai
items.blurb: Ain Dubai on Bluewaters Island is about 250 m tall, the tallest Ferris wheel as of 2025.

items.name: Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge
items.blurb: The Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge carries a high-speed railway 164.8 km across China. It opened in 2011 and was still the longest bridge as of 2025.

items.name: 1915 Çanakkale Bridge
items.blurb: The 1915 Çanakkale Bridge across the Dardanelles in Turkey opened in 2022. Its 2,023 m main span is a nod to the republic's centenary in 2023. It was the longest suspension span as of 2025.

items.name: Millau Viaduct
items.blurb: The Millau Viaduct in southern France, opened in 2004, has a mast summit 343 m above the valley floor, taller than the Eiffel Tower. It was the tallest bridge as of 2025.

items.name: Gotthard Base Tunnel
items.blurb: The Gotthard Base Tunnel under the Swiss Alps, opened in 2016, is 57.1 km long, with up to 2.3 km of rock above it. It was the longest railway tunnel as of 2025.

items.name: Lærdal Tunnel
items.blurb: Norway's Lærdal Tunnel, opened in 2000, is 24.5 km long. Three big caves with blue lights break up the drive. It was the longest road tunnel as of 2025.

items.name: Channel Tunnel
items.blurb: The Channel Tunnel between England and France, opened in 1994, is 50 km long, about 38 km of it under the sea.

items.name: Three Gorges Dam
items.blurb: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River in China can produce 22,500 megawatts, the largest power station as of 2025.

items.name: Narendra Modi Stadium
items.blurb: The Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad, India, reopened in 2020 with about 132,000 seats, the most of any stadium as of 2025.

items.name: Melbourne Cricket Ground
items.blurb: The Melbourne Cricket Ground holds about 100,000 people, the largest stadium in Australia and in the Southern Hemisphere as of 2025.

items.name: Trans-Siberian Railway
items.blurb: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs 9,289 km from Moscow to Vladivostok. The trip takes about a week and crosses eight time zones.

items.name: Trans-Australian Railway
items.blurb: The Trans-Australian Railway across the Nullarbor Plain has a perfectly straight stretch of 478 km, the longest in the world.

items.name: Qinghai–Tibet Railway
items.blurb: The Qinghai–Tibet Railway crosses the Tanggula Pass at about 5,072 m. Carriages have extra oxygen for passengers.

items.name: Arsenalna
items.blurb: Arsenalna station in Kyiv is about 105.5 m underground. It takes several minutes on two escalators to reach the platform.

items.name: Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport
items.blurb: Atlanta's Hartsfield–Jackson airport in Georgia, USA, has been the world's busiest by passengers almost every year since 1998, including the latest figures as of 2025.

items.name: Jupiter
items.blurb: Jupiter is about 143,000 km across at the equator, 11 times wider than Earth. More than 1,000 Earths would fit inside it.

items.name: Mercury
items.blurb: Mercury is about 4,879 km across, not much bigger than our Moon. It is also the planet closest to the Sun.

items.name: Saturn
items.blurb: Saturn is about 120,500 km across but is mostly hydrogen and helium; on average it is less dense than water.

items.name: Earth
items.blurb: Earth, about 12,756 km across, is the densest planet, at about 5.5 times the density of water, thanks to its big iron core.

items.name: Neptune
items.blurb: Neptune, about 49,500 km across, has winds of over 2,000 km/h, the fastest measured on any planet.

items.name: Longest day of any planet
items.blurb: Venus turns once every 243 Earth days, the slowest spin of any planet. Its year is only 225 Earth days.

items.name: Shortest day of any planet
items.blurb: Jupiter spins once every 9 hours 56 minutes, the shortest day of any planet, which makes it bulge at the equator.

items.name: Shortest year of any planet
items.blurb: Mercury goes round the Sun in 88 days, faster than any other planet.

items.name: Most known moons
items.blurb: As of 2025 Saturn had 274 known moons, far ahead of Jupiter. The count keeps rising as telescopes find small ones.

items.name: Ganymede
items.blurb: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is about 5,268 km across, wider than Mercury. It is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.

items.name: Titan
items.blurb: Saturn's moon Titan, about 5,150 km across, has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane.

items.name: Io
items.blurb: Jupiter's moon Io has hundreds of active volcanoes, heated by the tug of Jupiter's gravity.

items.name: Pluto
items.blurb: Pluto is about 2,377 km across, slightly wider than Eris, although Eris has a little more mass.

items.name: Ceres
items.record: Largest object in the asteroid belt
items.blurb: Ceres is about 940 km across and holds about a third of all the mass in the asteroid belt. It counts as a dwarf planet.

items.name: Olympus Mons
items.record: Tallest volcano in the Solar System
items.blurb: Olympus Mons on Mars is about 22 km high (measured from Mars's average surface level), more than twice the height of Everest above sea level.

items.name: Valles Marineris
items.record: Largest canyon in the Solar System
items.blurb: Valles Marineris on Mars is about 4,000 km long and up to 7 km deep; on Earth it would stretch across the United States.

items.name: Proxima Centauri
items.blurb: Proxima Centauri, a small red dwarf, is about 4.24 light years away. Light from it takes over four years to reach us.

items.name: Andromeda Galaxy
items.blurb: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light years away. It is the most distant thing most people can see with the naked eye.

items.name: Longest single spaceflight
items.blurb: Russian doctor Valeri Polyakov spent 437 days on Mir in 1994–95, the record for one trip as of 2025.

items.name: Most total time in space
items.blurb: Oleg Kononenko passed 1,000 days in space in 2024 and finished with about 1,111 days over five missions, the record as of 2025.

items.name: Voyager 1
items.blurb: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, left the Sun's bubble of solar wind in 2012 and was the farthest human-made object as of 2025, over 25 billion km away.

items.name: ThrustSSC
items.blurb: ThrustSSC, driven by RAF pilot Andy Green, reached 1,227.985 km/h in the Black Rock Desert, Nevada, in 1997, breaking the sound barrier. It was still the record as of 2025.

items.name: Spirit of Australia
items.blurb: Ken Warby drove Spirit of Australia, which he built himself, to 511.11 km/h on Blowering Dam, NSW, in 1978. It was still the record as of 2025.

items.name: Fastest human-powered vehicle
items.blurb: Canadian Todd Reichert pedalled the Aerovelo Eta, a fully enclosed recumbent bike, to 144.17 km/h in Nevada in 2016, the record as of 2025.

items.name: L0 Series
items.blurb: A crewed Japanese L0 Series maglev reached 603 km/h on its Yamanashi test line in 2015, the record for a crewed train as of 2025. In 2025 a small uncrewed Chinese test vehicle reached 650 km/h on a 1 km track.

items.name: TGV V150
items.blurb: A specially modified TGV called V150 reached 574.8 km/h on a line in eastern France in 2007, the wheeled-train record as of 2025.

items.name: North American X-15
items.blurb: In 1967 pilot William J. Knight flew the rocket-powered X-15 at 7,274 km/h (Mach 6.7), still the fastest flight by a crewed aircraft.

items.name: SR-71 Blackbird
items.blurb: A Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird flew at 3,529.6 km/h in 1976. The record has stood ever since.

items.name: Parker Solar Probe
items.blurb: NASA's Parker Solar Probe reached about 692,000 km/h when it swung past the Sun in December 2024, the fastest object ever made, as of 2025.

items.name: Airbus A380
items.blurb: The double-decker Airbus A380 can seat up to 853 people. It first flew in 2005; production ended in 2021.

items.name: Antonov An-225 Mriya
items.blurb: The six-engined Antonov An-225 Mriya could weigh 640 tonnes at take-off. The only one ever finished was destroyed near Kyiv in 2022.

items.name: Scaled Composites Stratolaunch
items.blurb: The Stratolaunch carrier plane has a wingspan of about 117 m, wider than a football pitch is long.

items.name: Seawise Giant
items.blurb: The supertanker Seawise Giant was about 458 m long, longer than the Empire State Building is tall. It was scrapped in 2010.

items.name: Largest animal ever
items.blurb: Blue whales can grow to about 30 m long and weigh up to about 190 tonnes, heavier than any dinosaur known.

items.name: Largest land animal
items.blurb: A big male African bush elephant can weigh about 6 tonnes and stand over 3 m at the shoulder.

items.name: Tallest animal
items.blurb: Giraffes can be about 5.5 m tall, tall enough to look into an upstairs window. Their necks have only seven bones, like ours.

items.name: Fastest land animal
items.blurb: Cheetahs can sprint at about 100 km/h or more, but only for a few hundred metres before they overheat.

items.name: Fastest animal (in a dive)
items.blurb: A peregrine falcon diving on its prey can pass 300 km/h, faster than any other animal.

items.name: Largest fish
items.blurb: Whale sharks can grow to about 18 m long, but they eat tiny plankton. Blue whales are bigger, but they are mammals, not fish.

items.name: Slowest mammal
items.blurb: Three-toed sloths move at about a quarter of a kilometre an hour and spend most of their lives hanging upside down in trees.

items.name: Longest-lived mammal
items.blurb: Bowhead whales live in Arctic waters. Old harpoon tips and eye studies suggest some live over 200 years.

items.name: Deepest-diving mammal
items.blurb: A Cuvier's beaked whale tagged off California in 2014 dived to about 2,992 m, and one stayed under for 3 hours 42 minutes.

items.name: Largest toothed whale
items.blurb: Male sperm whales can reach about 16–20 m. They hunt giant squid in the deep sea.

items.name: Largest dolphin
items.blurb: Orcas, also called killer whales, are actually the largest dolphins. Males can be about 8 m long.

items.name: Largest brain of any animal
items.blurb: A sperm whale's brain weighs about 8 kg, the largest of any animal, living or extinct.

items.name: Longest-lived vertebrate
items.blurb: Greenland sharks grow about 1 cm a year in icy water. Radiocarbon dating of their eyes suggests they live at least 272 years, maybe 400.

items.name: Fastest shark
items.blurb: Shortfin makos are the fastest sharks, with bursts often given as over 70 km/h, and they can leap out of the water.

items.name: Largest predatory fish
items.blurb: Great white sharks can grow over 6 m long. Larger whale and basking sharks eat only plankton.

items.name: Smallest shark
items.blurb: The dwarf lanternshark grows to about 20 cm, small enough to hold in your hand. It glows in the dark.

items.name: Deepest fish filmed
items.blurb: A young snailfish was filmed 8,336 m down in the Izu–Ogasawara Trench off Japan in 2022, the deepest fish ever recorded.

items.name: Largest bird
items.blurb: Ostriches can stand 2.7 m tall and weigh over 100 kg. They lay the biggest eggs of any living bird.

items.name: Smallest bird
items.blurb: The bee hummingbird of Cuba is about 5 cm long and weighs about 2 g, less than a coin.

items.name: Largest wingspan of any living bird
items.record: Largest wingspan of any living bird
items.blurb: Wandering albatrosses have wings up to about 3.5 m across and can glide over the Southern Ocean for hours without flapping.

items.name: Longest migration
items.blurb: Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, about 70,000 km or more, so they see two summers each year.

items.name: Deepest-diving bird
items.blurb: Emperor penguins can dive to over 500 m (535 m has been recorded) and stay under for about 20 minutes. They are also the largest penguins.

items.name: Highest-flying bird recorded
items.blurb: A Rüppell's vulture was sucked into a jet engine over Ivory Coast at about 11,300 m in 1973, the highest altitude a bird has been recorded at.

items.name: Largest egg relative to body size
items.record: Largest egg relative to body size
items.blurb: A kiwi egg can weigh about 15–20% of the female's body weight, the largest of any bird for its size.

items.name: Largest cat
items.blurb: Tigers are the largest cats; big Siberian (Amur) males can weigh over 250 kg.

items.name: Largest primate
items.blurb: Gorillas are the largest primates; a big silverback can weigh about 200 kg.

items.name: Largest rodent
items.blurb: Capybaras from South America can weigh over 60 kg. They are excellent swimmers.

items.name: Largest marsupial
items.blurb: Male red kangaroos can stand about 1.8 m tall and weigh up to about 90 kg.

items.name: Smallest mammal by mass
items.blurb: The Etruscan shrew weighs about 1.8 g. Its heart beats up to about 1,500 times a minute. (The bumblebee bat is the smallest by body length.)

items.name: Longest pregnancy of any mammal
items.blurb: Elephants are pregnant for about 22 months, nearly two years, the longest of any mammal.

items.name: Largest deer
items.blurb: Moose can stand over 2 m at the shoulder, and a bull's antlers can be about 1.8 m across.

items.name: Largest land animal in the Americas
items.record: Largest land animal in the Americas
items.blurb: A big male American bison can weigh about 1,000 kg. Tens of millions once roamed North America.

items.name: Largest reptile
items.blurb: Big male saltwater crocodiles can be over 6 m long and weigh over a tonne. They live from India to northern Australia.

items.name: Largest lizard
items.blurb: Komodo dragons from a few Indonesian islands can be 3 m long and weigh about 70 kg.

items.name: Longest snake
items.blurb: Reticulated pythons of Southeast Asia are the longest snakes, sometimes over 6 m. Green anacondas are heavier.

items.name: Heaviest snake
items.blurb: Green anacondas of South America can weigh well over 100 kg, heavier than any other snake.

items.name: Longest venomous snake
items.blurb: King cobras can grow to about 5.5 m, the longest venomous snakes. They mostly eat other snakes.

items.name: Largest turtle
items.blurb: Leatherback sea turtles can weigh over 500 kg. Instead of a hard shell they have a leathery back.

items.name: Largest tortoise
items.blurb: Galápagos tortoises can weigh over 400 kg and live over 100 years in the wild.

items.name: Largest frog
items.blurb: The goliath frog of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea can weigh over 3 kg. It builds little ponds for its eggs.

items.name: Oldest known living land animal
items.blurb: Jonathan, a giant tortoise on Saint Helena, hatched about 1832 and was the oldest known living land animal as of 2025, around 193 years old.

items.name: Largest spider by mass
items.blurb: The goliath birdeater, a tarantula from South America, can weigh about 175 g. Despite its name it rarely eats birds.

items.name: Largest spider by leg span
items.blurb: The giant huntsman spider, found in a cave in Laos in 2001, has legs that can span about 30 cm.

items.name: Largest butterfly
items.blurb: Queen Alexandra's birdwing from Papua New Guinea can have wings about 25 cm across.

items.name: Longest insect
items.blurb: A Chinese giant stick insect (Phryganistria chinensis) measured 64 cm with its legs stretched out, the longest insect known.

items.name: Most painful sting on the Schmidt index
items.record: Most painful sting on the Schmidt index
items.blurb: Entomologist Justin Schmidt gave the bullet ant's sting the only 4 in his original index: like walking over flaming charcoal with a nail in your heel. He later rated the tarantula hawk a 4 too, but its pain fades in about five minutes; a bullet ant's can last a day.

items.name: Largest arthropod on land
items.blurb: Coconut crabs can weigh about 4 kg with legs about 1 m across, and they can crack open coconuts.

items.name: Heaviest invertebrate
items.blurb: Colossal squid of the Southern Ocean can weigh about 500 kg. They also have the largest eyes of any animal, about the size of a football.

items.name: Largest crab by leg span
items.blurb: The Japanese spider crab can measure about 3.7 m from claw to claw. It lives in the deep waters around Japan.

items.name: Oldest individual animal (non-colonial)
items.blurb: Ming was an ocean quahog clam dredged up off Iceland in 2006. Counting the growth rings of its shell showed it was 507 years old.

items.name: Most venomous snake
items.blurb: The inland taipan of central Australia has the most toxic venom of any snake in lab tests, but it is shy and lives in remote places; no deaths have been confirmed since antivenom was introduced.

items.name: Most venomous marine animal
items.blurb: The Australian box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri) has up to 3 m tentacles covered in stinging cells, and a bad sting can kill an adult within minutes.

items.name: Most venomous fish
items.blurb: Reef stonefish look like rocks and have 13 venomous spines on their backs. Stepping on one is extremely painful and can be deadly.

items.name: Most poisonous frog
items.blurb: The golden poison frog of Colombia carries enough batrachotoxin in its skin to kill about ten adults. Indigenous hunters used it on blowgun darts.

items.name: Smallest dog breed
items.blurb: Chihuahuas, named after a Mexican state, usually weigh about 1.5–3 kg.

items.name: Fastest dog breed
items.blurb: Greyhounds can sprint at about 70 km/h. They were bred to chase hares.

items.name: Oldest cat on record
items.blurb: Creme Puff lived in Austin, Texas, from 1967 to 2005, reaching 38 years and 3 days, according to Guinness World Records.

items.name: Tallest man ever
items.blurb: Robert Wadlow of Alton, Illinois, was measured at 272 cm (8 ft 11 in) in 1940, shortly before he died aged 22.

items.name: Tallest woman ever
items.blurb: Zeng Jinlian of China was about 248 cm tall when she died in 1982 aged 17, the tallest woman on record.

items.name: Tallest living man
items.blurb: Sultan Kösen, a farmer from Turkey, was measured at 251 cm in 2011 and was still the tallest living man as of 2025.

items.name: Shortest adult ever verified
items.blurb: Chandra Bahadur Dangi of Nepal was measured at 54.6 cm in 2012, the shortest adult ever verified by Guinness World Records.

items.name: Oldest person ever (verified)
items.blurb: Jeanne Calment of Arles, France, lived 122 years and 164 days (1875–1997). She met Vincent van Gogh as a girl.

items.name: Oldest man ever (verified)
items.blurb: Jiroemon Kimura of Japan, a former post office worker, lived 116 years and 54 days (1897–2013).

items.name: Longest reign of a monarch (sovereign state)
items.record: Longest reign of a monarch (sovereign state)
items.blurb: Louis XIV, the "Sun King", ruled France from 1643, when he was four, until his death in 1715: 72 years and 110 days.

items.name: Longest-reigning British monarch
items.blurb: Elizabeth II reigned for 70 years and 214 days, from 1952 to 2022, passing Queen Victoria's 63 years in 2015.

items.name: Largest organ of the human body
items.record: Largest organ of the human body
items.blurb: Skin is the body's largest organ, about 2 square metres on an adult.

items.name: Largest internal organ
items.blurb: The liver weighs about 1.5 kg and does hundreds of jobs, from cleaning the blood to storing energy.

items.name: Longest bone
items.blurb: The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest and strongest bone, about a quarter of your height.

items.name: Smallest bone
items.blurb: The stapes, or stirrup, in the middle ear is about 3 mm long. It passes sound vibrations to the inner ear.

items.name: Largest muscle
items.blurb: The gluteus maximus in your buttocks is the largest muscle. It keeps you upright and powers climbing and running.

items.name: Hardest substance in the body
items.blurb: Tooth enamel is about 96% mineral and is the hardest substance the human body makes.

items.name: Longest nerve
items.blurb: The sciatic nerve runs from the lower back down each leg and is also the widest nerve in the body.

items.name: Highest skydive
items.blurb: Google executive Alan Eustace jumped from a balloon at 41,419 m over New Mexico in 2014, beating Felix Baumgartner's 2012 record. It still stood as of 2025.

items.name: Deepest scuba dive
items.blurb: Egyptian diver Ahmed Gabr reached 332 m in the Red Sea in 2014. It took him about 12 minutes to go down and nearly 15 hours to come back up safely. It was still the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most ascents of Mount Everest
items.blurb: Kami Rita Sherpa of Nepal reached the summit of Everest for the 31st time in May 2025, the record as of 2025.

items.name: Youngest Nobel Prize winner
items.blurb: Malala Yousafzai of Pakistan won the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize at 17 for her campaign for girls' education.

items.name: Oldest Nobel Prize winner
items.blurb: John B. Goodenough shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry at 97 for helping to invent the lithium-ion battery.

items.name: Most Academy Awards won by a person
items.record: Most Academy Awards won by a person
items.blurb: Walt Disney won 22 competitive Oscars (and four honorary ones), more than anyone else.

items.name: Most acting Oscars
items.blurb: Katharine Hepburn won four Best Actress Oscars (1934–1982). Meryl Streep and Daniel Day-Lewis have three each.

items.name: Most Oscars won by one film
items.record: Most Oscars won by one film

facts.holder: Ben-Hur, Titanic and The Return of the King

items.blurb: Ben-Hur (1959), Titanic (1997) and The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003) each won 11 Oscars.

items.name: Longest film ever made
items.blurb: Logistics by Erika Magnusson and Daniel Andersson runs 857 hours, about 35 days. It follows the journey of a pedometer back from Stockholm to the factory in China where it was made.

items.name: Longest-running theatre production
items.blurb: The Mousetrap opened in London's West End in 1952 and was still running as of 2025, apart from a break during the COVID-19 pandemic.

items.name: Longest-running Broadway show
items.blurb: The Phantom of the Opera ran on Broadway from 1988 to 2023, nearly 14,000 performances, the longest run as of 2025.

items.name: Longest-running TV soap opera
items.blurb: Coronation Street, set in a fictional street near Manchester, began in December 1960 and was still on air as of 2025.

items.name: Longest-running American animated series
items.blurb: The Simpsons began as a full series in 1989 and had passed 750 episodes as of 2025.

items.name: Longest-running science fiction TV series
items.blurb: Doctor Who began in 1963 and, counting the revival from 2005, was still running as of 2025.

items.name: Best-selling album
items.blurb: Michael Jackson's Thriller (1982) has sold an estimated 70 million copies worldwide.

items.name: Best-selling single
items.blurb: Bing Crosby's recording of Irving Berlin's "White Christmas" (1942) has sold an estimated 50 million copies, according to Guinness World Records.

items.name: Highest-grossing concert tour
items.blurb: Taylor Swift's Eras Tour (2023–2024) earned over $2 billion, the first tour to do so, and was the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most Grammy Awards
items.blurb: Beyoncé won her 35th Grammy in February 2025, the record for any artist as of 2025.

items.name: Best-selling book series
items.blurb: J. K. Rowling's seven Harry Potter books have sold over 600 million copies in more than 80 languages.

items.name: Best-selling fiction author
items.blurb: Agatha Christie's 66 detective novels and 14 short-story collections have sold an estimated 2 billion copies.

items.name: Most translated non-religious book
items.blurb: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince (1943) has been translated into more than 500 languages and dialects.

items.name: Best-selling manga
items.blurb: Eiichiro Oda's One Piece, running since 1997, had over 500 million copies in print as of 2025.

items.name: Best-selling video game
items.blurb: Minecraft, first released in 2009 by the Swedish studio Mojang, had sold over 300 million copies as of 2025.

items.name: Highest-grossing media franchise
items.blurb: Pokémon, started in Japan in 1996, had earned well over $100 billion across games, cards, TV, films and merchandise as of 2025.

items.name: Most expensive painting sold
items.blurb: Salvator Mundi, a painting of Christ attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, sold for $450.3 million at Christie's in New York in 2017, still the record as of 2025.

items.name: Most visited art museum
items.blurb: The Louvre in Paris had about 8.7 million visitors in 2024, the most of any art museum as of 2025.

items.name: Russia
items.blurb: Russia covers about 17.1 million km², stretching across 11 time zones from Europe to the Pacific.

items.name: Vatican City
items.blurb: Vatican City, inside Rome, covers about 0.49 km², smaller than many city parks. It is home to the Pope.

items.name: Most populous country
items.blurb: India passed China as the most populous country in 2023, with over 1.4 billion people; it was still first as of 2025.

items.name: Least populous country
items.blurb: Vatican City has only about 800 residents, mostly clergy and Swiss Guards.

items.name: Most densely populated country
items.blurb: Monaco squeezes about 38,000 people into about 2 km², nearly 19,000 people per square kilometre.

items.name: Largest landlocked country
items.blurb: Kazakhstan covers about 2.7 million km² of Central Asia without touching the open ocean (it borders the Caspian, a lake).

items.name: Longest coastline
items.blurb: Canada's coastline, around its mainland and tens of thousands of islands, is over 200,000 km long, the longest of any country.

items.name: Most time zones
items.blurb: France uses 12 time zones (13 counting its Antarctic claim) thanks to territories from French Polynesia to Réunion.

items.name: Largest country in Africa
items.blurb: Algeria covers about 2.4 million km², most of it in the Sahara. It became the largest in Africa when South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011.

items.name: Largest country in South America
items.blurb: Brazil covers nearly half of South America and borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.

items.name: Country with the most languages
items.blurb: Papua New Guinea has over 800 languages for about 10 million people, more than any other country.

items.name: Country with the lowest highest point
items.record: Country with the lowest highest point
items.blurb: The Maldives averages about 1.5 m above sea level, and its highest natural point is only about 5 m.

items.name: Most visited country
items.blurb: France welcomed about 100 million international visitors in 2024, the most of any country, as it had for decades, and it was still first as of 2025.

items.name: Northernmost capital of a sovereign state
items.record: Northernmost capital of a sovereign state
items.blurb: Reykjavík, Iceland, lies at about 64°N, the northernmost capital of a sovereign state. (Nuuk is farther north, but Greenland is part of Denmark.)

items.name: Southernmost capital of a sovereign state
items.record: Southernmost capital of a sovereign state
items.blurb: Wellington, New Zealand, at about 41°S, is the southernmost capital of a sovereign state.

items.name: Northernmost permanently inhabited place
items.blurb: Alert, on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada, is about 817 km from the North Pole. It has a few dozen staff and no permanent families.

items.name: Lowest city
items.blurb: Jericho in the West Bank lies about 258 m below sea level near the Dead Sea. It is also one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities.

items.name: Oldest university still operating
items.blurb: The University of al-Qarawiyyin was founded in Fez in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri. Guinness lists it as the oldest existing, continually operating university.

items.name: Oldest university in the English-speaking world
items.record: Oldest university in the English-speaking world
items.blurb: Teaching at Oxford dates back to at least 1096. Cambridge was founded in 1209 by scholars leaving Oxford.

items.name: Oldest restaurant
items.blurb: Sobrino de Botín in Madrid has been serving food since 1725; its wood-fired oven is said to have never gone out.

items.name: Oldest hotel
items.blurb: Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan in Yamanashi, Japan, was founded in 705 and has been run by the same family for over 50 generations.

items.name: Oldest company
items.blurb: Kongō Gumi was founded in 578 to build Buddhist temples in Osaka. Since 2006 it has been part of a larger construction firm.

items.name: Oldest national flag in continuous use
items.record: Oldest national flag in continuous use
items.blurb: The Dannebrog, Denmark's red flag with a white cross, has been used since the 1300s or earlier. Legend says it fell from the sky in 1219.

items.name: Oldest football club
items.blurb: Sheffield F.C. was founded in 1857 and is recognised by FIFA as the world's oldest football club. Notts County is the oldest professional club.

items.name: Oldest surviving film
items.blurb: Roundhay Garden Scene, filmed in Leeds in October 1888, lasts about two seconds and shows people walking around a garden.

items.name: Oldest of the Seven Wonders
items.blurb: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC, about 2,000 years before most of the other wonders.

items.name: Oldest Egyptian pyramid
items.blurb: The Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara was built around 2670 BC by the architect Imhotep, as six stacked steps.

items.name: Only Roman lighthouse still in use
items.record: Only Roman lighthouse still in use
items.blurb: The Tower of Hercules in A Coruña was built by the Romans in the 1st or 2nd century AD and still guides ships today.

items.name: Most expensive spice
items.blurb: Saffron is the dried stigmas of the crocus flower, picked by hand. It takes about 150,000 flowers to make 1 kg.

items.name: Most produced crop
items.blurb: About 1.9 billion tonnes of sugarcane are harvested each year, more by weight than any other crop. Brazil and India grow the most.

items.name: Women's World Cup titles record
items.blurb: The United States won the Women's World Cup four times (1991, 1999, 2015, 2019), the record as of 2025.

items.name: Euro titles record
items.blurb: Spain won Euro 2024 for their fourth title (1964, 2008, 2012, 2024), one more than Germany. It was the record as of 2025.

items.name: Copa América titles record
items.blurb: Argentina won their 16th Copa América in 2024, one more than Uruguay. It was the record as of 2025.

items.name: AFCON titles record
items.record: Most Africa Cup of Nations titles
items.blurb: Egypt won the Africa Cup of Nations seven times, the last in 2010. It was the record as of 2025.

items.name: Played at every men's World Cup
items.record: Only team at every men's World Cup
items.blurb: Brazil had played at all 22 men's World Cups from 1930 to 2022, the only country to do so as of 2025.

items.name: Cricket World Cup titles record
items.record: Most men's Cricket World Cup titles
items.blurb: Australia won the men's Cricket World Cup six times (1987, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2015, 2023), the record as of 2025.

items.name: Highest Rugby World Cup score
items.record: Highest score in a Rugby World Cup match
items.blurb: New Zealand beat Japan 145–17 in Bloemfontein at the 1995 Rugby World Cup. Simon Culhane kicked 20 conversions.

items.name: Most NBA MVP awards
items.blurb: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar won six NBA MVP awards (1971–1980), the record as of 2025. Michael Jordan and Bill Russell won five each.

items.name: Most Melbourne Cup wins by a horse
items.record: Most Melbourne Cup wins by a horse
items.blurb: Makybe Diva won the Melbourne Cup in 2003, 2004 and 2005, the only horse to win it three times.

items.name: Most Grand National wins by a horse
items.record: Most Grand National wins by a horse
items.blurb: Red Rum won the Grand National at Aintree in 1973, 1974 and 1977 and came second in the two years between.

items.name: Most Grand Prix motorcycle world titles
items.record: Most Grand Prix motorcycle world titles
items.blurb: Giacomo Agostini won 15 world titles in the 350 cc and 500 cc classes between 1966 and 1975.

items.name: Snooker century breaks record
items.blurb: Ronnie O'Sullivan made his 1,000th professional century break in 2019 and was still adding to the record as of 2025.

items.name: Fastest speed sailing record
items.blurb: Paul Larsen sailed Vestas Sailrocket 2 at 65.45 knots (about 121 km/h) over 500 m at Walvis Bay, Namibia, in 2012.

items.name: Danube
items.blurb: The Danube flows about 2,850 km from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea through ten countries and four capital cities.

items.name: Largest ice sheet
items.blurb: The Antarctic ice sheet holds about 60% of the fresh water on Earth. If it all melted, sea level would rise about 58 m.

items.name: Largest glacier
items.blurb: The Lambert Glacier in East Antarctica is about 400 km long and up to 100 km wide.

items.name: Largest salt flat
items.blurb: Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia covers about 10,600 km² high in the Andes, and holds a huge share of the world's lithium.

items.name: Largest river delta
items.blurb: The Ganges–Brahmaputra Delta in Bangladesh and India covers about 105,000 km². The Sundarbans, home to Bengal tigers, grow on it.

items.name: Tallest active geyser
items.blurb: Steamboat Geyser in Yellowstone National Park can erupt over 90 m high, but unpredictably, from days to decades apart.

items.name: Largest peninsula
items.blurb: The Arabian Peninsula covers about 3.2 million km² and includes Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, the UAE, Qatar and Kuwait.

items.name: European temperature record
items.blurb: A weather station near Syracuse in Sicily recorded 48.8 °C on 11 August 2021, confirmed by the WMO as Europe's record.

items.name: Highest temperature recorded in Antarctica
items.blurb: Esperanza Base on the Antarctic Peninsula recorded 18.3 °C on 6 February 2020, the WMO record for the continent.

items.name: Lowest temperature recorded in Australia
items.blurb: Charlotte Pass in the Snowy Mountains recorded −23.0 °C on 29 June 1994, Australia's official record low.

items.name: Australian temperature record
items.blurb: Oodnadatta in South Australia recorded 50.7 °C in January 1960, and Onslow in Western Australia matched it in January 2022.

items.name: Most snowfall in one US season
items.record: Most snowfall in one US season
items.blurb: The Mount Baker Ski Area measured 1,140 inches (95 ft, about 29 m) of snow between July 1998 and June 1999, the US record according to NOAA. The old record, 1,122 inches, was at Paradise on Mount Rainier in 1971–72.

items.name: Largest storm in the Solar System
items.record: Largest storm in the Solar System
items.blurb: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been raging for at least 190 years, and maybe since the 1600s.

items.name: Farthest planet from the Sun
items.blurb: Neptune orbits about 4.5 billion km from the Sun and takes about 165 Earth years to go round once. Pluto is no longer counted as a planet.

items.name: Most reflective body in the Solar System
items.record: Most reflective body in the Solar System
items.blurb: Saturn's moon Enceladus is covered in fresh ice that reflects almost all the sunlight that hits it. Geysers spray water from its south pole.

items.name: Largest space station
items.blurb: The International Space Station is about the size of a football pitch and has been lived on continuously since November 2000.

items.name: Most spacewalk time
items.blurb: Anatoly Solovyev made 16 spacewalks, mostly from Mir, totalling about 82 hours, the record as of 2025.

items.name: Largest single-dish radio telescope
items.blurb: China's FAST telescope in Guizhou, finished in 2016, has a 500 m dish built into a natural hollow. It was the largest single dish as of 2025.

items.name: Heaviest parrot
items.blurb: The kākāpō can weigh up to about 4 kg. It cannot fly, is active at night and is critically endangered.

items.name: Longest parrot
items.blurb: The hyacinth macaw is about 1 m long including its tail. Its huge beak can crack coconuts.

items.name: Largest penguin
items.blurb: Emperor penguins stand about 1.1 m tall and weigh up to about 45 kg. They breed in the Antarctic winter.

items.name: Fastest-swimming bird
items.blurb: Gentoo penguins can swim at about 36 km/h underwater, faster than any other bird.

items.name: Smallest primate
items.blurb: Madame Berthe's mouse lemur weighs about 30 g and could sit in an egg cup.

items.name: Smallest bat
items.blurb: Kitti's hog-nosed bat from Thailand and Myanmar is about 3 cm long and weighs about 2 g.

items.name: Largest wild dog
items.blurb: Grey wolves are the largest wild dogs; big males can weigh about 60 kg.

items.name: Largest seal
items.blurb: Male southern elephant seals can weigh up to about 4 tonnes. Their big noses help them roar.

items.name: Largest monkey

items.name: Most legs of any animal

items.name: Largest bee

items.name: Strongest bite measured

items.name: Petronas Towers

items.name: Largest mosque

items.name: Longest canal

items.name: Largest airport by area

items.name: Lowest capital city

items.name: Oldest complete piece of music

items.name: Oldest zoo still operating

items.name: Oldest amusement park
